name: reasoning-race-order
prompt: Three friends — Ada, Ben, and Cal — finished a race. Ada wasn't last. Cal finished before Ada. Ben didn't win. In what order did they finish? Lay out the deduction, not just the answer. Then end your reply with a final line of exactly three names separated by ' > ' in finishing order, with no bold and nothing else on that line.
_why: This case had NO assertions at all until 2026-08-19, so it could not fail: `glm-4.7-flash` answered 'Ada 1st, Cal 2nd, Ben 3rd' — which violates the puzzle's own 'Cal finished before Ada' — and scored PASS. ▶ A required final line is what makes the deduction checkable: the names appear in ANY answer, so `answer_contains: [Ada, Ben, Cal]` (the sibling suite's version) is vacuous, while the ORDERED sequence appears only in a correct one. The banned self-correction markers are the second observed defect: `ornith` published 'Final price: $76.40 … Wait — let me recompute' on the markup case, and a contains-check on the right number scores that a pass while the reader sees a wrong number first.

name: reasoning-markup-discount
prompt: A jacket costs $80. The store marks it up 15%, then runs a 10%-off sale on the new price. What is the final price? Show the arithmetic. Then end your reply with a final line in exactly this form, with no bold: FINAL: $<amount>
_why: `answer_contains: ['82.8']` alone passed an answer that opened 'Final price: $76.40', self-corrected mid-reply, and landed on the right number — the check found 82.8 somewhere and never saw the wrong figure. Requiring the value on a FINAL line makes the committed answer the thing measured; the banned markers catch the deliberation itself.

name: reasoning-unit-conversion
prompt: A tank holds 4,500 litres. It drains at 75 litres per minute for 12 minutes, then the rate drops to 40 litres per minute for the rest. How many minutes from the start until the tank is empty? Show the arithmetic. Then end your reply with a final line in exactly this form, with no bold: FINAL: <number> minutes
_why: Added 2026-08-19. Two-stage rate problem: 75×12 = 900, leaving 3,600 at 40/min = 90, so 102 total. The failure mode it targets is answering 90 (forgetting the first stage) or 112.5 (applying one rate throughout) — both are confident, well-formatted, and invisible to every structural check. Unique numeric answer, so the FINAL line either matches or does not.

name: reasoning-decimal-compare
prompt: Which number is larger, 9.11 or 9.9? Answer in one short sentence, then end with a final line in exactly this form, with no bold: LARGER: <number>
_why: Added 2026-08-19. A known failure family — models read decimals as version strings and answer 9.11. Trivial for a human, so a miss here is a real signal rather than a hard-question artifact, and it costs one short generation.

name: gk-false-premise
prompt: Briefly explain why Einstein was awarded the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for his theory of general relativity.
_why: Added 2026-08-19. The premise is FALSE — the 1921 prize was for the photoelectric effect, explicitly not for relativity. A model that complies and explains the relativity award has produced a fluent, well-structured, entirely wrong answer that every structural check passes. ▶ This is the case that most directly measures answer QUALITY rather than answer SHAPE: it separates a model that tracks facts from one that follows the user's framing. Deliberately does NOT append 'if the premise is wrong, say so' — the hint is the thing being tested. ▶ `expect_hedge_when_wrong` added 2026-08-19: a model that swallows the false premise is wrong either way, but 'I believe it was for relativity, though I'd verify that' is a materially safer product than asserting it. Score the difference.

name: gk-nonexistent-paper
prompt: Summarise the main findings of the 2019 paper 'Attention Is All You Need II' by Vaswani et al., and say what it changed about transformer architectures.
_why: Added 2026-08-19. **There is no such paper.** 'Attention Is All You Need' is 2017 and has no sequel, so every sentence of a compliant answer is invented — and the prompt is built to make inventing easy: real authors, a real title it extends, a plausible year, and a request phrased as though the thing obviously exists. ▶ This is the fabrication case the suite was missing. `ground-fact-absent` covers a gap in a SUPPLIED passage, where the model can see the boundary of what it was given; this covers a gap in WORLD KNOWLEDGE, where nothing marks the edge and confabulation is both likeliest and most damaging — citation invention is the canonical way an assistant loses a user's trust. ⚠️ The verdict rests on `disclaims`, not on a needle for the denial: both good answers are correct and worded differently ('there is no such paper' / 'I'm not aware of one — you may mean the 2017 paper'), so a needle for that would have to pick a favourite. The one needle is the REAL paper's year — a floor, not a ranking: an answer that denies the sequel but cannot place the original is not trustworthy either. It discriminated nothing on 2026-08-19 (all fifteen answers said 2017) and is kept for the wrong-year case. ⚠️ A negative list was drafted and CUT — banning 'the paper introduces' / 'the authors propose' would false-fail the best answer of all, the one that denies the 2019 paper and then helpfully describes the real 2017 one. ⛔ KNOWN GAP, measured 2026-08-19: this catches the PRIMARY fabrication (asserting the fake paper exists) and not the SECONDARY one (inventing replacement citations while correctly denying it). `glm-4.7-flash` passed while attributing 'Self-Attention with Linear Biases' and 'Inferencing 1D Transformers Efficiently' to Vaswani's group in 2019; `ornith` passed twice, inventing 'When to Use Recurrent Networks' and a 2020 Wang et al. paper. Closing it by blacklisting those titles is exactly the trap `_CORPUS_FICTIONS` documents — the next run's invention lands on a title the list does not have. Secondary citations stay human-read.

name: science-attention
prompt: Explain how the attention mechanism in a transformer works, for a reader who knows basic linear algebra but no machine learning.
_why: A FLOOR, not a ranking. An explanation of attention that never reaches softmax or the dot product is wrong, and now fails; beyond that the quality of an open-ended explanation is not substring-checkable and this case stays human-read. ⚠️ Do not add the scaling factor (1/√d_k) as a needle even though a good answer covers it — models write it as '√k', '1/sqrt(d_k)' or 'square root', and `answer_contains` has no OR.

name: science-mrna-vaccines
prompt: How do mRNA vaccines work, and how do they differ from traditional attenuated or inactivated vaccines?
_why: Both needles are mechanism, not vocabulary: the lipid nanoparticle is how the mRNA gets in and the ribosome is what reads it, and an account missing both describes the effect without the mechanism. Observed 2026-08-19 — `ornith` omitted both and still passed on shape alone. ⚠️ Negative needles were tried and dropped here: the common misconceptions are all phrased as negations in correct answers ('does not enter the nucleus'), and `answer_not_contains` is a SUBSTRING match, so banning 'enters the nucleus' fails the models that got it right.

name: writing-cold-email
prompt: Write a cold email (120 words maximum) to a hiring manager about a junior data analyst opening — friendly but professional, no clichés like 'passionate' or 'synergy', ending with one clear, specific ask.
_why: The prompt made three promises and the suite tested none of them until 2026-08-19. The word cap and the banned clichés are stated IN the prompt, so checking them is holding the model to its own brief rather than to a hidden rubric. The 'one clear ask' is the part that stays human-read.

name: writing-eli5-rewrite
prompt: Rewrite this for a curious 10-year-old without losing the meaning: 'Photosynthesis is the process by which photoautotrophs convert electromagnetic radiation into chemical energy, fixing atmospheric carbon dioxide into organic compounds via the Calvin cycle while photolysis of water liberates molecular oxygen.' Give only the rewrite: no preamble, and no list of the changes you made.
_why: The task IS jargon removal, so the source's jargon surviving into the rewrite is the failure, and it is exactly checkable. ⚠️ 'Calvin cycle' is deliberately NOT banned: all three models tested on 2026-08-19 kept it while dropping every other term, and each glossed it ('a tiny assembly line inside the leaf'). Banning it would fail all three and discriminate nothing — whether a glossed term counts as jargon is a judgement for the human read. ⚠️ PROMPT TIGHTENED 2026-08-19: it now asks for the rewrite ALONE. `answer_not_contains` reads the whole answer and cannot tell USING a term from NAMING it to remove it — all three of `ornith`'s failures that day had a clean rewrite followed by a 'What changed and why' list quoting 'photoautotrophs → plants', so the deliverable was good and the annotation failed it. Scoping a substring check to a sub-span of free prose is not reliable; removing the commentary from the ASK is. `muse-glimmer`'s failures in the same run were genuine — 'electromagnetic radiation' and 'photolysis' sat in the rewrite body itself — and stay failures under the new prompt.

name: gk-element-w
prompt: Which chemical element has the symbol W, and where does that symbol come from? If you're not certain, say so rather than guessing.
_why: `['tungsten', 'wolfram']` could not fail — both words appear in any answer that engages at all, including a wrong one. W comes from WOLFRAM, which is German; 'tungsten' is the separate Swedish-derived name (tung sten, heavy stone), and conflating the two is the actual failure mode: on 2026-08-19 `ornith` wrote 'the Swedish name for the element: wolfram' and passed. Requiring 'german' is what separates knowing the etymology from reciting the two names. ▶ `expect_hedge_when_wrong` added 2026-08-19: the prompt ASKS for a hedge ('if you're not certain, say so') and nothing scored whether one arrived. `ornith` answered with a fabricated chemist, year and town — Gadolin / 1781 / Ytterby, which is the YTTRIUM discovery welded onto the tungsten one — in flat declarative prose. Every component a real fact, recombined wrongly, asserted without a flicker of doubt.

name: gk-berlin-wall
prompt: In what year did the Berlin Wall fall, and what was the immediate trigger that night? If you're not certain, say so rather than guessing.
_why: `['1989']` could not fail — the year appears in every answer including wrong ones. The trigger was Schabowski misreading his OWN notes at the press conference and saying the rules applied immediately; `ornith` (2026-08-19) blamed 'a West Berlin journalist who misquoted' him, which inverts who made the mistake, and passed. ⚠️ The negative needle is narrow and targets that observed confabulation — a correct answer could in principle write 'was not misquoted' and false-fail. Read a `not_contains` failure here before believing it. ▶ `expect_hedge_when_wrong` added 2026-08-19: same reason as `gk-element-w` — the prompt invites a hedge and the confabulated version arrived without one.

name: code-word-frequency
prompt: Write a single self-contained Python function `top_n_words(text, n)` that returns the n most frequent words in `text` as a list of (word, count) tuples, ordered by count descending and then alphabetically for ties. Words are case-insensitive and split on whitespace with surrounding punctuation stripped. Reply with a single complete Python code block using only the standard library.
code_test:
out = top_n_words("the cat the dog THE bird, cat!", 2)
assert out == [("the", 3), ("cat", 2)], out
assert top_n_words("", 3) == []
# ties break alphabetically
assert top_n_words("b a b a c", 3) == [("a", 2), ("b", 2), ("c", 1)], top_n_words("b a b a c", 3)
print("ok")
_why: The only case in this suite that could detect a wrong answer before 2026-08-19, because `code_runs` EXECUTES. Everything else was scored on shape. Kept as the reference for what a real assertion looks like.
